title: No honourable and sincere man, said Stephen, has given up to you his life and his youth and his affections from the days of Tone to those of Parnell, but you sold him to the enemy or failed him in need or reviled him and left him for another. And you invite me to be one of you. I’d see you damned first
html_source: Stephen also rejects Irish nationalism because he feels its people have turned their backs on their own leaders. Wolfe Tone and Charles Stewart Parnell, both prominent Protestant Irish leaders for an Independent Ireland, were betrayed (or at least abandoned) by their own when the chips were down. Tone was a founding member of the United Irishmen, but was eventually caught and imprisoned. He committed suicide before he was due to be executed. Many other United Irishmen met the same fate, such as Henry Joy McCracken, a Presbyterian who was hanged in his own native Belfast. Around this time the United Irishmen had begun to dissolve due to growing issues between Protestants (primarily Ulster Scots Presbyterians who made up the bulk of the movement) and Catholics, who at this time both considered themselves as being Irish. Likewise, when Parnell’s affair was brought to light, many of his supporters abandoned him and turned their back on him. Stephen finds Irish nationalism faulty because he sees its people as being so quick to turn on their own leaders or to let their disagreements eradicate their goals.
